Metformin XR — Mean PK Profiles & Absorption Mechanisms (PBPK)

Why AUC∞ destabilises and Tmax plateaus as dissolution T50 increases

Author

Nikita

Published

June 9, 2026

Purpose

This report shows the population mean plasma concentration–time profiles of metformin XR across the dissolution-T50 sweep (1–7 h) and uses them to explain two features seen in the PK-parameter sweep:

  1. AUC∞ behaves erratically (inflates, with exploding CIs) at high T50.
  2. Tmax stops increasing — it plateaus (~4–5 h) — at high T50.

Both trace to the same physiology: as release slows, metformin enters flip-flop kinetics and runs up against its finite intestinal absorption window.

Mean concentration–time profiles (all T50 overlaid)

Inference. As T50 increases the peak falls and broadens (linear panel) — slower input spreads the same-ish amount of drug over more time. The semi-log panel is the key: the fast-release curves (purple) show a clear, steep terminal decline (true elimination), whereas the slow-release curves (yellow/green) are flat in the tail and actually cross above the fast curves by 24 h. A terminal slope that flattens with slower release is the textbook signature of flip-flop kinetics — the tail is now governed by ongoing slow absorption, not elimination.

Inference. Three things move together: Cmax halves (29.9 → 13.2), Tmax saturates at 4.25 h, and the fraction absorbed by 24 h falls from 81% to 51%. Meanwhile the 24 h concentration barely changes (~2.9–3.3) — relative to a falling Cmax, the tail is increasingly sustained, i.e. flip-flop.

Fraction of dose absorbed over time

Inference. Every curve plateaus below 1.0 — absorption is incomplete, and more so the slower the release. Metformin is absorbed mainly in the upper small intestine (a finite absorption window); once the dosage form transits past that window, the still-undissolved drug is never absorbed. Slow release therefore loses a growing fraction of the dose (F: 81% → 51%), which is exactly why Cmax and AUC₀-t decline.

Q1 — Why does AUC∞ go wild at high T50?

(Note: it is AUC∞ that misbehaves; AUC₀-t declines smoothly and is well behaved.)

Mechanism.

  • Flip-flop inflates the terminal half-life. Metformin’s true elimination t½ is ~6–9 h. As input slows below the elimination rate, the observed terminal slope reflects absorption, so the apparent t½ balloons (8.6 → 36 h). Tell-tale: CL/F stays flat (~2.5) while Vz/F quadruples — because Vz/F = (CL/F)/λz and λz collapses; the volume isn’t really changing.
  • λz is fitted on a phase that isn’t truly terminal. At T50 = 7 h the curve is still rising/flat at 24 h (the tail sits above the fast-release arms). NCA fits a shallow, ill-defined λz and extrapolates Clast/λz to infinity — and that tail is now 47% of AUC∞. A 47% extrapolation off an unreliable λz is essentially noise, so AUC∞ and its between-subject CI blow up (population AUC∞ at 7 h had a 90% CI of ~[1.0, 3.1] and even produced non-finite t½/Vz/F for some subjects).
  • AUC∞ should be flat, so the rise is the giveaway. AUC∞ = F·Dose/CL; CL is fixed and F falls, so a true AUC∞ can only stay flat or decline. Its apparent rise is purely the extrapolation artefact — not extra exposure.

Consequence for the BE work: we lead with AUC₀-t, which is truncation-honest and smooth. To rescue AUC∞ for the slow arms, re-run T50 ≥ 5 h out to ~72–96 h so absorption completes and a real terminal phase emerges (driving %-extrapolated back under ~20%).

Q2 — Why does Tmax plateau (~4–5 h) at high T50?

Mechanism. Two effects, both visible above:

  • The peak becomes a broad plateau. Spreading the input flattens the top of the curve (the ≥95%-of-Cmax window is several hours wide), so Tmax becomes a shallow, weakly-defined maximum that no longer tracks release rate.
  • Tmax is gated by the absorption window, not by dissolution. Beyond a certain slowness the peak occurs around the time the dosage form transits out of the upper-GI absorption site — a roughly fixed ~4–5 h — regardless of how much slower the remaining drug dissolves. Past that point, slower release does not delay the peak; it simply leaves more drug unabsorbed (the falling F above), lowering Cmax and AUC₀-t while Tmax stays put.

Summary

Bottom line. Slow release pushes metformin into flip-flop, window-limited absorption. Use AUC₀-t (not AUC∞) for the XR safe space; expect Tmax to saturate; and if AUC∞ is ever required, extend the slow-arm simulation duration so the terminal phase is real.
